to declare to you and to the world in a concise manner that Robert, in the invention of his Harmony and the arrangement of its proportions, did not err as gravely as you perhaps thought at first glance. But before I descend into the discourse of my own Harmony, I will now speak of the Harmony of the ancients, for two reasons that compel me to do so. First, to indicate to the learned that I am not altogether as ignorant of the Harmony of the ancients as I have been portrayed by John in many places. Second, to adapt the proportions of their Harmony more correctly and easily to my monochord of the world, so that you (most esteemed readers) might judge more correctly regarding that comparison of mine.

We find it recorded that both the world and its souls were to be described most conveniently through harmonic proportions, according to both the Pythagoreans and the Academics. And since there were three kinds of melodies, or harmonies, primarily in use and practice among the ancients: namely the Diatonic, which proceeded in all tetrachords (previously discovered for the arrangement of the four elements) by a Tone, a Tone, and a Semitone, constituting the <term>Diatesseron</term> <gloss>a musical interval of a perfect fourth</gloss>—which kind is somewhat harsh, but still natural. The Chromatic, receding from the Diatonic (or natural) and resonating more softly, decreases by a semitone, a semitone, and three semitones, which, when joined, also make a <term>Diatesseron</term>. And finally the Enharmonic, which is sung in all tetrachords by a <term>Diesis</term> <gloss>here taken as a quarter-tone</gloss>, a <term>Diesis</term>, and a ditone, which, when all added together, also measure the <term>Diatesseron</term> consonance. From these, that divine Plato chose the Diatonic for describing his Harmony of the world and the soul, perceiving that this kind is more natural, simple, and generous, and consequently more disposed in itself to represent and describe originally the symphonic offices and harmonic proportions of the world and the soul—that is, the connection between aquatic matter and lucid form, or the passive and the active—in each case by itself and in relation to one another. He was all the more induced to this choice because it was observed by him and Timaeus of Locri that this kind has in its nature a certain governance of rational life, just as the Harmonic governs every body adapted to life, and the Chromatic has a regard for the corporeal idea. But since reason is more eminent and noble among these properties of the soul, and this Diatonic kind is more natural in its arrangement, he chose it above the others for this inquiry into worldly Harmony.

But just as the ancients proceeded through this in tetrachords, so Plato, in imitation of Nicomachus, expanded it to the nature of the heptachord <note>a seven-stringed instrument or scale</note>, conformed to seven limits, for a better and more proportional demonstration of his Harmony. He began from unity and doubled it up to the binary cube, namely 8, and then afterwards tripled it up to the cube and solid of the ternary. According to the proportion of such numbers, therefore, the Academics thought the fabric of both the soul and the world to have been arranged and brought to completion, according to those ancient teachings of Pythagoras, who equated the proportions of the ternary number to the soul, as the masculine, acting perfection and to light, just as he equated those of the binary to matter, as to imperfection, the feminine, the passive, and to water. From the conjunction of these—that is, from matter and form—all things were created and propagated in this world. The most learned in numerical science therefore adapted the <term>Monad</term> <gloss>the number one/unity</gloss> to God the Creator, the <term>Dyad</term> <gloss>the number two/duality</gloss> to matter, the virgin <term>Triad</term> <gloss>the number three</gloss> to the forms themselves, and the <term>Heptad</term> <gloss>the number seven</gloss> to life and man. Hence Plato arranged his Diatonic Harmony to the heptachord because he adapted it to both internal worlds, that is, to the soul and to corporeal substance, the proportions of which he deduces from the aforementioned 1, 2, 3. The cubes of these numbers complete the structure of both the soul and the world: the cube of the ternary, namely 27, for the soul; and the cube of the binary, namely 8, for the body or matter.

But these proportions in the fabric of the world, as it seems to me, are best understood from the account of the prelate Moses: "The Spirit of the Lord moved upon the waters." This spirit of the Lord is formal unity, just as the waters are material unity. Then the doubling took place when the Creator commanded that universal matter be informed, saying: "Let there be light." Then the square of this binary was produced when that general mixture was reduced into the four elements, which were dispersed throughout the vast cavity of the world. Finally, through the cube of that binary, the bodies of creatures were propagated: namely, the stars from the mixture of celestial elements, and minerals, vegetables, and animals from those sublunary ones. And in this proportional way, material creation was completed, and the female in this world according to the arrangement of the three dimensions, namely length, breadth, and depth—that is, line, surface, and body—which correspond in the greater world to the most tenuous substance of the Empyrean heaven, to that of the middle, and to the Elemental, whose relations, as we have said in our Harmony, are to the root, the square, and the cube in the binary number. Finally, all the intervals of those numbers are filled with ternary numbers of the same proportion, without which they cannot exist; for without these, a vacuum and emptiness would follow in the feminine mass. Whence in Genesis all created things are said to be good and filled with divine rays, insofar as they participate in the goodness of the Elohim—that is, the Holy Spirit, arguing for the ternary number in the divine property—without which all things would be, as they were before its appearance, darkness and void. Therefore, one must proceed by the masculine force (the ternary) in the same proportion as the feminine up to the cube; for it was this masculine virtue that attributed degrees and proportions to the feminine substance, filling its intervals with life, essence, and action, and establishing the most perfect harmony in the world. Specifically, the proportion of the most perfect consonance, the <term>Diapason</term> <gloss>the octave</gloss>, in the angels and the intellectual spirit, which is in double proportion, such as 1 and 2; and the less perfect one, the <term>Diapente</term> <gloss>the perfect fifth</gloss>, in the Olympian demons and the ethereal heaven; and the imperfect <term>Diatesseron</term> in lower things, such as in animals, vegetables, and minerals. To these three regions of the world, therefore, belong these three enneads <note>groups of nine</note> arranged as follows:

<meta>continues from previous page: ...to the seekers of fame; or if they are filthy hunters of money, as if schools were opened only to acquire such things; or if they are gluttons, debauched, and mired in a life of pleasure; or finally if they are deceitful, those for whom literature is a poison of the mind, when it should be its medicine, and who are cunning deceivers; or if they are marked by any other crime of this kind, we completely and utterly forbid all of them from these sacred things. For it is better for them if they remain hidden in the perpetual darkness of ignorance than if they seek support for their wickedness from the arts, or if, while they pursue their vices, they put on the appearance of virtue in order to deceive the ignorant. It will also be better for the disciplines if they never touch them, so that by abusing them they do not bring about their corruption. But we shall move on to the reasons that compel me to think in this way.</meta>

<margin>Reason I. Because the Kingdom of God must be sought from the beginning.</margin>

§. IV. That one necessary thing, to <term>seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness</term> <note>original: "ζητεῖν τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ τὴν δικαιοσύνην αὐτοῦ" (Matthew 6:33)</note>, if we believe in God, if we believe in Christ, must be postponed to nothing, and it ought to be preferred to all things; why then should it not be preferred to the arts and sciences, however great they may be? And this warning should be enough for us, considering the authority of the one who gives it. Let this single rule, as if fallen from heaven, be the one for the knowledge of all things, by which we may direct all our actions, as well as the order of our studies, their beginning, and their end. Let us measure any precepts of wisdom by this standard, and finally, let us ascertain this law before we lend our ears to any doctrine of mortals. And because this is not merely a piece of advice from the Savior, but His commandment, it does not require reasoning, but obedience. Yet, reasons are not lacking here, which we must now <margin>Reason II. Because all good arts are from God.</margin> bring to light. Plato denies that the truth of things, which depends on God, can be held unless the truth about God Himself is held (t). He is truly a sad prophet of his own philosophy; whose teacher, the true God...

¶ A round figure has no corners. The heart is therefore round so that matter harmful to the body cannot be retained within it. Otherwise, according to Aristotle, it is answered that a round figure is apt for motion, and therefore, according to Aristotle, a round figure is metaphorically called <term>agononia</term> <gloss>without corners</gloss>, from 'a', which means 'without', and 'gonia', 'angle', as if to say 'without an angle'.
¶ It is asked: Why is blood made in the heart alone, by excellence? It is answered that blood is in it as in its primary place, or as in its efficient cause, which others say of the liver. Whence the heart receives blood from no member, but other members receive it from the heart.
¶ It is asked: Why do some animals not have a heart? It is answered that although they do not have a heart, they still possess something proportionate to a heart, as is evident in fish and eels, which have backbones instead of a heart.
¶ Why, as we see by sense in brute animals, such as geese and chickens, when their heads are amputated, does the heart still pulse and live? It is answered that the vital spirit remains in it longer than in other members, because the heart is the first to live and the last to die, as Aristotle says in his work *On Youth and Old Age*. Therefore, the heart pulses and moves longer than other members.
¶ It is asked: Why does every animal lacking a heart, or a part proportionate to a heart, lack blood, as is evident in flies? It is answered that the heart is the principle of blood; now, with the cause lacking, the effect also fails.
¶ It is asked: Why does the pulse of the heart judge more certainly on the right side than on the left? It is answered that the heat of the heart creates greater ability and heat there, and so it feels more there than on the left side.
¶ It is asked: Why does the heart sometimes faint, as is evident in those who fall or are epileptic? It is answered, according to Constantine in his book *On the Stomach*, that this happens from a defect of the heart itself and the membranes by which it is covered, by which the heart is then infected and faints. Sometimes it happens from the infection of neighboring members. Whence, when poisonous humor arises from the orifice of the stomach, it harms the heart and the members near to it, and then these induce fainting in the heart. ¶ It is to be noted, according to Aristotle, that the disposition of the heart is known most of all by the pulse of the heart, because a fast, large, and frequent pulse testifies to the heat of the heart and a good complexion, while a slow and weak pulse testifies to the coldness of the heart and a bad complexion. <sig>Ec</sig>

Regarding this, Silius says in his eighth book:

> Meonia, once the glory of the Vetulonian race:

> And it added as many axes in silent terror.
> This city adorned the high curule chairs of ivory,

<margin>Vetulonia <term>Wete-loon</term>.</margin>

<margin>Viterbum.</margin>

Where this city was once located, I do not see that there is agreement among writers. However, it pleases most people that Viterbum was made from <term>Longhola</term>, Vetulonia, and Tyrrhenian Volturna by Desiderius. Regarding this matter, he who wishes to indulge in the dreams of an old man may consult Annio, who tortures himself wonderfully regarding the reason why Desiderius named the city Viterbum. To us, this is most clear: since <term>Viter-bou</term> signifies nothing other than a more ample structure, which he made while he surrounded three ancient small towns with one wall, even including the spaces in between them, so that there is no need for the Cabalistic trifles of Annio, who, just as he brought forward various opinions about the name of Viterbum, so he no less tortured himself regarding the letters F.A.V.L., which marks Desiderius permitted to be struck on Viterbian coins. But not even in these did anyone find anything that in any part approaches the truth, let alone touches it. We do not have the necessity to examine things which are more recent than those Ogygian times. It is enough to have called that city by its ancient name of Vetulonia, from which it is revealed that magistracies among the Etruscans were rewards for knowledge, not for nobility or riches. I suspect in the meantime that <term>Longhula</term> was in the beginning merely a suburban village of Vetulonia, in which insignia were given to him who was about to enter the magistracy, adorned with which he would enter Vetulonia. For <term>Loon</term> signifies reward; <term>gesul</term>, and syncopated <term>g'hul</term>, signifies an inauguration, by which someone receives some public power through a solemn rite. Whence it happens that they strayed very little who judged that <term>Longhula</term> of the Etruscans should be written with an aspiration in the second syllable, even if they were ignorant of the reason, even if it had to be done. I think <term>Volturna</term> was called so concisely from <term>Voltorrena</term>, because it was full of towers, for armament and war machines, and then also for preserving the security of the prince of the city. Vetulonia therefore indicates to us by its name that it is true, which, along with others, Diodorus writes, that the greatest rewards, not only of other things but also of military discipline, were established among the Tyrrhenians, in whose monuments this is especially to be noted, and to be held by all princes and cities as the most illustrious example, that the greatest and most splendid honors are owed not to riches, not to the nobility of birth, not to favor; but to knowledge alone and to the skill of administering the republic well both at home and abroad. I wish that the entire Christian world deserved the name of Vetulonia: we would not have these calamities by which we are oppressed, and the destructions of entire regions. But farewell to laments that will profit nothing. Since, therefore, the foundations of other arts and of this civil science, by which men are made fit to hold the helm of peace and war well, were being laid among the Volsinians, it was most rightly and piously done that Vortumnus was invoked among them most of all, because he promoted the studies of the boys in such a way that from them as many as possible would emerge worthy of the highest honors.

When, however, this statue was transferred to Rome, and by whom, I do not see to be very clear. To Propertius, Annio seems to be understood in such a way that he wished it to have been brought by Lucumo, bringing aid to Romulus; because he says that Vortumnus does not regret having deserted Volsinii during the battles. These words, however, can be taken in such a way that he says he does not regret, among the battles, that he migrated to Rome; because the virtue of the Romans shone forth most in battles.

But because we do not blush to attend to our own affairs, and we labor through conscience and strive not through contention, so that they may also think better, and that our own people may not be seduced away by worse things, we freely bring forward whatever needed to be said regarding the account of the faith for which we are accused. And even if this is difficult for us, for we hold nothing established by them, we are compelled to review all our affairs that could come to mind, upon which to excuse ourselves. It could happen that we spoke more regarding those things which they least desired, while we spoke less of those things which they most wished to be treated. But by that conscience which now, after I have voluntarily descended against them, who could have kept me in silence, I believe is seen by all, I testify that I have voluntarily passed over nothing which I thought would satisfy them sufficiently. Therefore, if anything is said less by us than their desire, this shall proceed from their own dissimulation, since it depended only upon their own suspicion, so that we might conjecture what it was that the wickedness of others could find to disapprove in us. I see, therefore, two points out of two. The envy of violated faith is stirred up against us, I think; that which we observe concerning the magnificence, ornament, and wealth of the temples, and that which we observe concerning the dispensation of the sacraments and the whole order of divine office. I see that these can be blamed for two reasons: either because they are against the law of God and the decrees of the ancestors, or because they are matter for vice in the wicked. Therefore, if ecclesiastical rites are rejected because of the latter, it is not yet proven that doing the same is against the law of God; furthermore, the first leaders of religion ought not to have instituted the same rites for that same Waldensian reason. But if they did institute them, with what counsel they instituted them, by that same counsel they shall be preserved by us. For it would be a great iniquity that things which are holy by their own right should be condemned by the vice of a few. But if some judge this to be fair, I will in turn judge it to be fair that the same rites should be preserved by the innocence of the better. Therefore, let the Waldensian cast all this innocence away from us, yet because he thinks himself to be good, and knows that he, being good, knows well how to use good things, for that confidence, and also for the reverence of the ancestors, he should not cast away those holy things, nor prostitute them, but preserve those which would have corrupted through the vices of our people. For they will be found to be guilty and prevaricators of the apostolic sanctions. But even if ecclesiastical rites were an occasion for evil to the wicked, they shall not be condemned for that reason. For what is holy anywhere, which the perverse would not wish to use badly? That I may not seek long examples: you have railed against canonical scriptures for the contempt of the virgin mother of God, for the dishonor of the saints, for the impious opinion of the purgation of souls, and for the weaving of heresy. Let us then also say some such thing about the scriptures. We do not hold them, therefore, because they are for the subversion and error of the faith. Let us turn the figure of speech back to you. You have held our ecclesiastical rites in contempt because of our vices, as you say. You, therefore, because of the Manichean and every impurity of heresy, will also despise the holy scriptures from that opinion of yours, saying: "We do not receive them because they have been for the subversion of the faith and justice to the Manichean." You see horns growing against you from the opposite side, you see the madness of your own mind. I will say other things so that you may be clearly apprehended. You cast I know not what impediments to justice. Shall I, therefore, throw away my dead unburied because I know an undertaker will redeem a harlot with my money? An impure word, but their stupidity provokes me, which, from equal just things, has been thought to have come from a similar crime of the priests, which they have brought forth publicly once and again. Regarding our ceremonies, while they neither name them nor say by whose authority they are reprehensible, they claim they are not worthy of reprehension. But because we do not blush to address our own affairs, and because we labor with conscience and strive not with contention, we move voluntarily to provide whatever reasons must be spoken regarding the faith for which we are accused, so that they may perceive things better and our own people may not be seduced from them by inferior things. And although this is difficult for us, as we have nothing established by them to which we might excuse ourselves, we are forced to recount all our own practices that have come to mind. It may happen that we say more about matters they least desired, or speak less about those they most wished to be discussed. 

But by that conscience which I believe is now observed by all, since I have come down to them voluntarily, whereas I could have held myself in silence, I testify that I have omitted nothing that I thought would satisfy them significantly. Therefore, if something is less discussed by us due to their desire, this will stem from their own dissimulation, since it relied only upon their own suspicion, so that we might guess what it was that their perceived impropriety could find to disapprove in us. I see, therefore, two things out of two that provoke the envy of violated faith against us: namely, those things which we observe regarding the magnificence, ornamentation, and wealth of churches, and those regarding the administration of sacraments and the entire order of divine office. 

I see that these can be accused for two reasons: either because they are against the law of God and the decrees of our ancestors, or because they serve as matter for vice for the wicked. If, therefore, ecclesiastical sacraments are rejected for the latter reason, it has not yet been proven that the same are done against the law of God. Furthermore, it would not have been fitting for the first leaders of religion to institute those same sacraments for that same Waldensian reason. But if they did institute them, they will be kept by us with the same intention; for it would be a great iniquity if things that are holy by their own right were condemned due to the vice of a few. But if some think this is just, I, in turn, will think it just that the same sacraments be preserved by the innocence of better men. 

Therefore, why should the Waldensian completely reject all this innocence from us? Because he thinks himself good, and thinks he knows well how to use good things for the good, he ought not to cast out those holy things—nor prostitute them—but preserve what might have perished through the vices of our own people. For they will find both the guilty and the violators of apostolic sanctions. But even if ecclesiastical sacraments were an occasion for evil for the wicked, they would not on that account be condemned; for what is holy is holy everywhere, lest the perverse should wish to use it badly. 

To not seek long examples, you, because of your contempt for the Virgin Mother of God, your dishonoring of the saints, and your impious opinion concerning the purgation of souls, have been refuted by canonical scriptures as a heretic. Let us therefore say the same thing about the scriptures. We do not contain them because they result in the subversion and error of the faith. Let us turn the figure of the argument against you. You have despised our ecclesiastical sacraments because of our vices, as you say. You, therefore, because of the Manichean <note>referring to a dualist heresy</note> and the entire impurity of heresy, will you also despise the sacred scriptures for that same opinion of yours? Suppose you say: "We do not receive them because they have served the Manichean for the subversion of faith and justice." You see the horns growing against you from the opposite side; you see the madness of your own mind. 

I will say other things so that you may be clearly caught. You throw about I know not what "impediments to justice." Shall I therefore cast out my dead, unburied, because I know that a funeral director will use my money to redeem a prostitute? It is an impure word, but the stupidity of those people provokes me, who, because they have thought that equal things were just if they originated from the similar wickedness of priests, have previously declared them openly once and again. We expose laws and impious things for gain, therefore let them be announced: the priests, the leaders of the Mosaic law <note>the Law of Moses</note>, were abusing them for avarice. Let us abolish Judaism before Christ abolishes it on his cross!

Since they say our ceremonies are not condemned, though they state neither which ones nor by whose authority they are reprehended, we are not ashamed to address our own affairs. Because we labor with a clear conscience and strive not with contention, and because we desire that they might perceive better things—and that our own people might not be seduced by worse things—we willingly put forward an account of the faith for which we are accused, explaining whatever needed to be said on the matter. Even though this is difficult for us, since we have no established list of complaints from them, we are forced to review all our own practices that have come to mind. It may have happened that we spoke at greater length about things that were least desired, while speaking less about those things they most wanted to address. But by the conscience that I think is now apparent to all—having come down to them willingly, though I could have kept myself in silence—I testify that I have intentionally left out nothing that I thought would sufficiently satisfy them. Therefore, if anything is missing from our statement due to their desire, this will stem from their own dissimulation, since it depended only on their own suspicion, requiring us to conjecture what it was that their impropriety could find to blame in us.

I see, therefore, two things out of two that stir up envy of the violated faith against us: the first concerns the magnificence, adornment, and wealth of the temples; the second concerns our observance of the distribution of the sacraments and the entire order of divine office. I see that these can be accused for two reasons: either because they are against the law of God and the decrees of the ancients, or because they are a source of vice for the wicked.

Now, if the ecclesiastical sacraments are rejected for the latter reason, it has not yet been proven that the same are done against the law of God. Furthermore, it was not appropriate for the first leaders of religion to institute the same sacraments for that same Waldensian reason. If they did institute them, they shall be preserved by us with the same intention, for it would be a great iniquity if things that are holy by their own right were condemned due to the vice of a few. But if some think this is just, I, in turn, will think it just that the same sacraments be preserved through the innocence of the better ones. Therefore, if the Waldensian rejects all this innocence from us entirely, he should not, because he thinks himself to be good and knows how to use good things well, cast out or prostitute those holy things out of that confidence and reverence for the ancients. Rather, he should preserve them, even if they had corrupted through the vices of our own people. For they will be found to be transgressors of apostolic sanctions.

Neither shall ecclesiastical sacraments be condemned if they have been an occasion for evil to the wicked. For what is holy exists everywhere, even where the perverse may not want to use it well. Not to seek long examples: you, out of contempt for the Virgin Mother of God, for the dishonoring of the saints, and for the impious opinion regarding the purgation of souls, have been babbling against the canonical scriptures in order to construct a heresy. Let us therefore also say something similar about the scriptures: we do not hold them because they result in the subversion and error of the faith. Let us turn the figure of speech against you. You have held our ecclesiastical sacraments in contempt on account of our vices, as you say. You, therefore, on account of the Manichaean <note>original: "Manicheum"; a reference to the dualist sect of Mani, often used as a polemical label for heresy</note> and all the impurity of heresy, will also hold the sacred scriptures in contempt according to your sentiment, saying: "We do not receive them because they were, for the Manichaean, a subversion of faith and justice." You see the horns growing against you from the opposite side; you see the insanity of your own mind.

I will say other things so that you may be clearly caught. You throw out I know not what impediments to justice. Should I therefore throw away my dead and unburied, because I know the undertaker will redeem a prostitute with my money? It is an impure word, but I am provoked by their foolishness, which has argued that those things, once thought to be equal and just, were from the similar crime of the priests, which they have publicly proclaimed once and again. We expose the laws and the impious for the sake of profit, therefore let them be declared: the priests, leaders of the Mosaic law <note>original: "Mosayce legis"</note>, used the same for avarice. Shall we take away the Judaism that Christ himself did not take away upon his cross?

VIII. Finally, if one of the extremes and the middle is found in the nature of things, the other is also accustomed to being found. In the universe of things, a certain highest <term>foelicitas</term> <gloss>happiness/felicity</gloss> is found, and again, a certain condition joined with some unhappiness; therefore, a certain highest unhappiness will also be found, and likewise something affected in a middle way, such as the happiness and unhappiness of this life. IX. Nor does the fiction of the Platonists or the <term>Origenistarum</term> <gloss>Origenists</gloss> provide support, which claims that the act of sin and the lust joined to it are momentary. For even if the act and the little pleasure joined to the act pass away, the stain, however, and the inclination to sin left behind by the sin, remain perpetually. Even if neither of these remained, it is still neither new nor unusual, not only in natural things but also in moral ones, for that which is accomplished in a moment or certainly in a very brief time to leave behind a perpetual trace.

Eight (says <term>Augustinus</term> <gloss>Augustine</gloss>) kinds of punishments, writes <term>Tullius</term> <gloss>Cicero</gloss>, exist in the laws: loss, chains, blows, retaliation, ignominy, exile, death, and servitude. The second first intention <note>referring to a concept of the second order</note> is a mental term naturally signifying a thing, not a term: such as the mental term "human," "John," or "stone," which naturally signify a thing as to its being, and not terms.
<margin>Simple Apprehension</margin>
There is another opinion held by the Scotists, who say that second intentions are not mental terms; rather, a second intention is a relation or a respect of reason caused by the comparative act of our intellect, by comparing one thing in order to another.
<margin>Scotus, Book 1, dist. 13.</margin>
For the clarification of this, it must be noted that there is a twofold act of the intellect. Namely, simple [apprehension], through which something is known simply and absolutely, not in relation to another. The other is a comparative act, through which something is known in relation to another: such as the act of the intellect by which I know a human in relation to an animal, or to something else; and through such an act, second intentions are caused.
<margin>This proposition is found in Scotus, Q1, Q4, where he says that the [non-being] is not compared to the exterior except through some proper [property] found in itself.</margin>
The second first intention is an object known as knowable, not caused by the comparative act of the intellect, upon which it is the nature of a second intention to be founded, or to which it is the nature of a second intention to be attributed; and other propositions follow from these.
<margin>Scotus, Book 1, dist. 8, q. 4; Scotus, Book 1, dist. 13.</margin>
First: second intentions are never founded in one, nor are they attributed to anything, except according to the known being of that thing.
<margin>Scotus, q. 7, Quodlibeta.</margin>
Second proposition: these second intentions are never attributed to anything except by reason of some property found in it. From which it follows that the intellect cannot attribute any second intention to Peter, except only that which can belong to him by reason of some property.
<margin>in itself is...</margin>
Third proposition: second intentions do not have being <note>existence</note>; therefore, this should not be conceded: "second intentions are." It is proven: because second intentions have no more truth or perfection of being than those things to which they are attributed, or in which they are founded; but those things to which they are attributed, under that aspect by which they are attributed, have only a known being, of which this verb "is" cannot be verified as existing in itself and adjacently; for this is not granted: "Adam is"; thus, it should not be granted of second intentions, which are founded in them.

From these, other corollaries follow.
<margin>Scotus, q. 3, Quodlibeta.</margin>
First: that in order for us to have knowledge of something, it is not required that it have real being, but it suffices that it have known being; for of a non-existent rose we can have true knowledge, and also of second intentions, which do not exist.

It follows secondly that those second intentions do not inhere in anything, taking "inhere" properly, but only diminutively; nor are they in another as a subject properly: because for something to be in another subjectively and properly, it must be a being, and that in which it inheres must also be a being.

And if someone says: what is said to Avicenna, who says that logic is about second intentions joined to first ones? It is answered: that second intentions are not joined to first ones according to inherence, but only according to denomination, or as it were objectively by way of a mode: so, namely, that second intentions or the terms of second intentions are predicated of first ones by extrinsic denomination.

It follows thirdly: that those who say that second intentions move the intellect partially, and cause their intellections or notions partially, do not speak well, but they offer a way to sustain that the Antichrist and even a chimera cause something; because second intentions have no more real being than the Antichrist or a rose that does not exist. Thus, to cause is a true act of a real being, as has been seen; therefore, it cannot belong to anything except a real being.

There remains a small difficulty: for someone might ask whether second intentions are intelligible per se. It is answered that they are. And if someone says: they do not fall under the object of our intellect, which is real, created, limited being. It is answered that second intentions are contained per se virtually under the adequate object of our intellect, namely in first intentions; for then they are known. Something is said to be contained virtually in another and in known being in two ways. In one way, immediately, as a property is immediately contained virtually according to known being in a subject. In another way, subsequently or oppositely: and thus I say that second intentions are contained virtually in first ones, so that they are known in first

<column-break/>

intentions, in such a way that by all intentions, by reason of some properties found in them, they cause the cognitions of those second intentions: therefore they are contained in the first [intentions] virtually.

## It is doubted thirdly
whether logic is useful, honorable, and necessary for the acquisition of other sciences. For this doubt, certain distinctions and other statements are posited.
<margin>useful good</margin>
**First distinction:** of goods, one is honorable, one useful, and one delightful.
**Second distinction:** a useful good is spoken of in four ways.
**First**, a useful good is called that which is not desirable for its own sake but only for the sake of another, without which, however, that other cannot be acquired: as walking after dinner is called useful in this way; it is not desired for itself, but for health, without which, however, such health cannot be acquired.
**In the second way**, a useful good is called that which is not desirable only for itself, but for the sake of another, without which, however, that other cannot be well acquired; and in this way, food is a useful good: because it is not desirable for itself, but for another, namely for extinguishing hunger, without which such an extinguishing of hunger cannot be well had; and in these two ways, logic is not useful.
<margin>3rd way</margin>
**In the third way**, a useful good is called that which is desirable for itself and also for the sake of another, without which, however, that other can be acquired: as a sweet potion is called useful in this way; because it is desirable for itself and also for another, namely for health, without which, however, health can be acquired.
<margin>4th way</margin>

## CHAPTER II.
## Presenting the first part of <term>pragmatologia</term> <gloss>the science of facts or objective reality</gloss>, namely
# THE DEFINITION OF AN AXIOM.

### THESIS I.

The definition of an axiom presented by the most venerable Weisenbach <note>referring to Johann Michael Weisenbach</note> in his *Nucleus Logicae*, § 228, is commonly approved by philosophers.
> An axiom is an indemonstrable proposition, so evident that you can possess knowledge of it even before instruction. This also finds its foundation in Aristotle, *Posterior Analytics*, Book 1, Chapter 2, § 14, and his interpreters on this passage, who should be consulted.

### THESIS II.

In the cited definition, the genus is posited as an "indemonstrable proposition," which it shares in common with a thesis taken in the stricter sense, which Aristotle, in the aforementioned location, divides into definition and hypothesis. It is called <term>anapodeiktos</term> <gloss>indemonstrable</gloss>, or that which cannot be demonstrated, not because it admits no demonstrations whatsoever—for we know that axioms presuppose sensory cognition, and likewise are demonstrated <term>a posteriori</term> <gloss>from effect to cause</gloss> through reduction to the impossible (excepting the absolutely first principles), through refutation or debate <term>kat' anthropon</term> <gloss>according to human reasoning</gloss>, and induction—but because it does not admit demonstrations <term>dioti</term> <gloss>of the cause/why</gloss> (which are saluted as demonstrations in the absolute sense). # THE DEFINITION OF AN AXIOM.

### THESIS I.

> An axiom is an indemonstrable proposition, so evident that you can possess knowledge of it even prior to formal instruction. This also finds its foundation in Aristotle, *Posterior Analytics*, Book 1, Chapter 2, § 14, and his interpreters on this passage, who should be consulted.

### THESIS II.

In the cited definition, the genus is posited as an indemonstrable proposition, which it shares in common with a thesis taken in the stricter sense, which Aristotle, in the aforementioned work, divides into definition and hypothesis. It is called <term>anapodeiktos</term> <gloss>indemonstrable</gloss>, or that which cannot be demonstrated; this is not because it admits no demonstrations whatsoever—for we know that axioms presuppose sensory cognition, and are likewise demonstrated <term>a posteriori</term> <gloss>from effect to cause</gloss> through reduction to the impossible (with the exception of the absolutely first axiom), through refutation or debate <term>kat' anthropon</term> <gloss>according to man/human perspective</gloss>, and through induction. Rather, it is because it does not admit demonstrations <term>dioti</term> <gloss>demonstrations of the cause/why</gloss> (which are strictly hailed as demonstrations). This is because such a proposition is primary, either absolutely or in a relative sense, and enjoys a universal nature—if not objectively, then subjectively—(even if the universal sign does not always formally and expressly exist, for example, in the statement "The whole is greater than its part"). Thus, a progression into infinity is not undeservedly rejected. See Stahl, *Institutiones Logicae* <gloss>Institutes of Logic</gloss>, Book 5, Chapter 2, § 15, and Stratemann's *System*.

Here, thrown down, not so much at the feet, as our customs and senses. pro Cæl. 54. A cast-down and tearful groan. 2. Tusc. 97. A man held in contempt and cast down. contra Rul. 85. Plainly cast down and broken. 11. fam. 30. For he himself is cast down by an equal fortune. epist. l. 4. 13. 3. The daughter cast down by fear. in Catil. 118. A humble and cast-down speech. in Or. 112. You have crushed the madness and petulance of a cast-down and effeminate man. in Pis. 24. He aroused the cast-down man. 1. Att. 41. He aroused the cast-down man as much as he could. 5. Att. 42. A man whom we saw held in contempt and cast down at Rome. in Rul. 91. That he would be cast down and humbled unless he were restored through you. Lentulo, lib. 1. 5. 13. A private citizen should be neither submissive nor cast down, nor, etc. lib. 1. Off. 173. He raised up the state, cast down even by fear, to some hope of liberty. pro Dom. 20. I do not think that such a cast-down hope of composition is the most desperate. 9. Att. 26. in ep. Balbi. They think nothing cast down, nothing humble. 5. de Fin. 103. To be of a struck and cast-down mind. 40. Att. To do something with the hesitation cast aside. Off. 115. Clodius, having cast aside his toga, threw himself at the feet of his son-in-law. 55. Att. Broken and cast down. 4. fam. 25. When we ourselves are cast down and neglected among ourselves. de Fin. l. 3. 53. The cast-down hexameters of the comic poets. in Or. 107. Words not cast down. de Cla. 186. If we despise this, we also consider those to be cast down. Acad. q. ed. 1. lib. 2. 121. In some, the spirit is more cast down. de Amic. 107. That I shall be of a more cast-down spirit. Lent. lib. 1. 9. 56.

### Abiecte.
That we may not do anything in a cast-down manner. Tusc. 387. Nor did I bear it in a cast-down manner. 3. Phil. 143.

### Abiectio.
What is the weakening and casting down of your spirit, etc. in Pis. 69.

### Abintegro.
Whether you think there is less work to create one new column from scratch, with no recycled stone, or to replace those four. 3. Ver. 104.

### Abiudico.
Where I find more evil than good, I judge that entirely away and reject it. de Or. l. 2. 57. He will judge that Alexandria belongs to the king, he will judge it away from the Roman people. de Leg. Agr. 51. To judge something away from someone. contra Rul. 74. Nothing which was not judged away from him, by the power of that man. 2. Ver. 8. To have liberty judged away from oneself. pro Cæcin. 72. The account of truth judged away from this order. in Ver. 77.

### Abiungo.
Demosthenes separated himself from this obstructionist judicial style of speaking. 2. Att. 2.

### Abiuro.
It is more certain for me to forswear than to pay out. 1. Att. 15. Tuscul. lib. 3. 14.

### Ablego.
This (embassy) sends me away from my brother's arrival. Att. lib. 2. 33. 4. He employed those whom he had sent away. in Ver. 125. Let those who know the case send them away. in Ver. 125.

### Ablegatus.
The council having been dismissed and sent away. 4. Ver. 52. The man having been removed and sent away. 7. Ver. 66.

### Ablegatio.
That speech, no doubt, demands some sending away. 1. de Leg. 14.

### Abluo.
Your most illustrious grandsons washed away the cruelty of their enemies with their own blood. ad Her. 28. The disturbance of the mind is washed away by placation. Tusc. 222. They are tossed by waves so that they are never washed away. pro S. Rosc. 30.

### Abluens.
Washing the feet of Ulysses. 5. Tusc. 66.

### Abnuo.
I do not refuse, I do not deny. pro Mil. 77. For your will never denied anything to my zeal. Fat. 4. You may understand what anyone concedes, what he denies. 2. de Fin. 5. To deny that a crime was committed by oneself. de Leg. 164. You deny that you are being approached. 3. de Or. 90.

Tractatuum volumen primum.

236 ¶ And the Clerk. Regarding civil law: if anyone appeals from a sentence of excommunication while the appeal is pending, he is not excommunicated, for by the appeal the pronouncement is rescinded. <note>original: "l. j. in fine. ff. ad turpilianum."</note> And because once an appeal is made he is exempted from the jurisdiction of the one who passed the sentence, it does not bind him in the meantime. <note>original: "l. si. ff. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum. l. si a non competenti."</note> However, it is also permitted to appeal from a sentence that carries execution with it. <note>original: "ff. de poenis. l. qui ad statuam. l. qui ultimo."</note> In canon law, however, a distinction is made: either the excess was in the day or under a condition, then if he appeals, the effect of the excommunication does not last in the meantime; or it is passed unconditionally, and in this case he remains excommunicated even if an appeal is pending. <note>original: "c. praeterea. c. pastoralis. de appellationibus."</note>

237 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, while restitution <note>a legal process to restore the original state of affairs</note> is pending, nothing is to be innovated, nor is the sentence ordered to be executed in the meantime. <note>original: "C. nil novari in integrum restitutione pendente. in rubrica magis"</note> But in canon law, the sentence is ordered to be executed while the question of restitution is pending, provided that a security is posted to revoke everything retroactively if it happens that the benefit of restitution is granted. <note>original: "c. sciscitata. de in integrum restitutione."</note> Or regarding the presumption there against one seeking restitution, as noted in the said chapter *Sciscitata*. And to this effect, <note>original: "c. de falsis. l. satis."</note>

238 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, if several are in disagreement, the sentence of the majority prevails. <note>original: "ff. de re iudicata. l. duo ex tribus."</note> But in canon law it is not so, for in a criminal case the sentence of the majority does not suffice, even if twelve were of a unanimous opinion. <note>original: "v. q. viij. si quis episcopus. no. de reg. iur. in vj."</note>

239 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In canon law, prescription <note>the acquisition of a right through the passage of time</note> runs for the entire time the alienator or dilapidator is in bad faith. <note>original: "xv. q. iij. si sacerdotes."</note> But in civil law, we do not have good faith if prescription runs immediately after the alienation. <note>original: "aut quas actiones. C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. Regarding civil law: those things which are held by enemies are granted to the occupants, as are things which are in the goods of no one. <note>original: "insti. de re. di. §. item lapilli."</note> But in canon law, in places held by enemies, a Roman bishop cannot occupy a diocese or his own parish unless it is granted to him by a superior. <note>original: "c. cum de perba. tibi per Innocentium."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. Whoever flees in public war is punished by capital punishment by civil law. <note>original: "ff. de re militari. l. omnem."</note>

242 §. When in the battle line. <note>original: "q. in acie."</note> But in canon law, he is infamous. <note>original: "vj. q. j. infames."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. If someone has bequeathed in a legacy <note>a bequest</note> that it is hindered, he delivers it so that he may be the servant of the enemies. <note>original: "ff. de legationibus. l. si."</note> But in canon law, he is excommunicated. <note>original: "xxiij. q. ult. si quis."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, if someone has changed the cause of his possession, the laws which we have hold place. <note>original: "C. de acquir. possess. l. cum nemo. s. l. ex liberis. et que in eis notatur."</note> But in canon law, if someone has changed the cause of possession in basilicas, he is to be deprived of his benefices as unworthy. <note>original: "c. illud. de excess. praela."</note>

244 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, a blasphemer is punished with the ultimate penalty, as in the <term>autentica</term> <gloss>a collection of Justinian's constitutions</gloss> regarding those who do not act against nature. <note>original: "ut in aut. ut non luxu. contra naturam."</note> But in canon law, specifically, he is excommunicated, and if a cleric, he is deposed. <note>original: "xvij. q. iiij. c. si quis per capitula etiam iponit poenam prout tradit de clericis maledicis. c. si quis in otio."</note>

245 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, if someone uses false instruments and repents, he is not punished for forgery. <note>original: "C. de fal. l. falsos."</note> In canon law it is otherwise regarding apostolic letters. <note>original: "c. cura. c. ad falsariorum. de fal. si modo literis non sint o simplici iustitia. c. accedens."</note>

246 regarding forgeries. ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, the crime of rape is committed against a betrothed woman. <note>original: "C. de rap. virg. l. j."</note> But in canon law it is otherwise. <note>original: "extra de raptoribus. c. cum causam."</note>

247 ar. 27th question, 2nd question, §. 1st. ¶ And the Clerk. In civil law, he who has corrupted a virgin is heavily punished, yet he is not forced to take her as a wife; rather, it is prohibited by the power of matrimony between them, in the <term>autentica</term> <gloss>a collection of Justinian's constitutions</gloss> regarding the rape of women. <note>original: "in aut. de rap. muli."</note> But in canon law, he is compelled to receive her as a wife. <note>original: "248 re. c. h. de adul."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, a very bitter penalty is imposed on the murderer of children. <note>original: "l. j. C. de his qui par. vel libe. occi."</note> But in canon law, he is not punished in that way, as in the chapter regarding infants who killed their children. <note>original: "in c. de infantibus. de his qui filios occiderunt."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, the penalty for forgery is deportation and the confiscation of all goods, and this for a free man; for a slave, it is the ultimate punishment. <note>original: "l. j. §. ult. ff. de fal fis."</note> But in the canons, the penalty for forgery is manifold, according to the many types of forgery, as Hostiensis notes in his *Summa* regarding forgeries. <note>original: "§. poena falsi."</note>

250 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, he who has ceded his goods can recover them in their entirety. <note>original: "ff. qui bonis cede. pnt. l. is qui."</note> But in canon law, once the license to cede the episcopal dignity has been obtained, he is compelled to cede it. <note>original: "c. quidam. de renunciatione tibi 251 reddidit rō iter."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, fame alone would not impede matrimony from being performed: because when there is not full proof, but semi-full proof. <note>original: "ff. de testa. l. ij. not. in l. in bone fidei. C. de iureiur."</note> But in canon law, public fame alone, which knew the consanguinity <note>blood relationship</note> of the future bride or wife, would impede the matrimony from being contracted. <note>original: "c. super eo. de consangui. et affini. c. cum intua. de sponsalibus."</note>

252 fall. ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. The voice of one witness does not impede matrimony from being contracted in civil law. <note>original: "l. iurisiurandi. C. de testibus."</note> But in canon law, if the mother alone of one desiring to contract matrimony asserts consanguinity between them, it impedes the matrimony. <note>original: "c. sup eo. de testibus."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, there is a certain penalty of the mines; those who are condemned to the mines are afflicted with heavier chains. Others are in the work of the mines, and these are affected by lighter ones; both of these lose their citizenship and liberty. Others, however, are condemned to the service of the miners and serve entirely in the mines, and these lose their citizenship but not their liberty. This is done for the time they are condemned. If, however, it is in perpetuity, they lose both citizenship and liberty. <note>original: "ff. de pe. l. aut damna. §. cui poena."</note> In canon law, such penalties are not found imposed, nor should they be. <note>original: "c. de calumniatis."</note> But to these penalties can be equated the penalty of prison, which the Church inflicts for grave crimes, <note>original: "c. plene. r. c. ff. de hereticis."</note> and the penalty by which one is reduced to servitude, <note>original: "xvij. q. iiij. c. si quis."</note> or handed over to the court to serve, <note>xj. q. j. statuimus."</note> or otherwise sold. <note>original: "l. r. vi. de clerici."</note>

254 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, a boy or girl who has attempted to know <note>to engage in sexual intercourse</note> before seven years, and perhaps could not on account of the weakness of age, by this introduces the justice of public decency, so that matrimony cannot be contracted. <note>original: "c. iuvenis. de sponsalibus."</note> But in civil law, it is not found among the causes that impede matrimony, which causes are enumerated in the law <note>original: "l. iij. D. de nupt. circa finem. et insti. de nupt. §. h."</note> And similarly, if a brother has betrothed someone de facto, who by law could not because of impeding consanguinity with the other brother, he cannot contract matrimony. <note>original: "c. ad audientiam. de sponsalibus."</note> But in civil law, there is no bond through prior betrothal impeding consanguinity, for where it is impossible, there is no obligation. <note>original: "§. si impossibile. insti. de inuti. stipula."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, regularly, delay <note>a technical term for failure to fulfill an obligation on time</note> does not occur by the thing itself, but by interpellation made in a suitable place and time. <note>original: "ff. de usur. l. mora. in princ. et ibi fallit in casibus ibi notatis."</note> But in canon law, delay occurs by the thing itself in the slow payment of tithes. <note>original: "xvj. q. j. in 256 decime. not. in. c. cum homines. de decimis."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, simple fornication is not punished; rather it is permitted. <note>original: "l. in concubunatu. ff. de concubi. l. ij. C. de donat. inter virum et uxorem."</note> By canon law, every fornication is prohibited. <note>original: "xxiij. q. iiij. nemo sibi. et ibi not."</note>

257 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, matrimony is dissolved if one of the spouses wishes to enter a monastery, and does enter. <note>original: "in aut. de nup. §. dissolvatur."</note> 258 But in the canon it is otherwise. <note>original: "xxvij. q. ij. Agatosa."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, nuptials can be contracted between first cousins. <note>original: "C. de nup. l. in celebrandis. q. non. l. iij. ca. q. ij."</note> He who is related in the fourth degree of consanguinity or affinity is prohibited from contracting matrimony. <note>original: "c. non est de consangui. et affini."</note>

259 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, paternal power lasts throughout the entire age of the son. But in canon law, paternal power is dissolved upon reaching adult age regarding carnal and spiritual matrimony, which pertains to an oath. <note>original: "xx. q. ij. puella. xxiij. q. iij. tribus not. xxij. q. v. honoretur."</note>

260 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, a man is not permitted to beat his wife. <note>original: "l. cosenſu. C. de repudijs."</note> Nevertheless, he can correct her. <note>original: "vij. q. j. scilicet alterius. l. respiciendum. ff. de penis."</note> But in the canons, it is only permitted to clerics to guard, bind, and compel their wives who are sinning to fasts, yet not to mortify them. <note>original: "xxiij. q. iiij. placuit. et est ratio in clericis potior quam in aliis, ut ibi not."</note>

261 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, a wife cannot vow continence, nor the opposite, without the license of the other spouse. <note>original: "xxxiij. q. v. c. j. et ij."</note> By canon law it is otherwise: for matrimony is broken if one wishes to vow chastity, in the <term>autentica</term> <gloss>a collection of Justinian's constitutions</gloss> regarding nuptials. <note>original: "in aut. de nup. §. dissolvatur."</note>

262 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In canon law, if someone proposes a peremptory exception after the actor's intention has been established, and it happens that he fails in the proof of that exception, he is condemned to the actor for expenses. <note>original: "c. finem litibus. et ibi not. de dolo et contuma."</note> But in civil law, that which is said about the condemnation of expenses does not have a place, except in a specific case, so that the loser is condemned by the winner for expenses. <note>original: "C. de iudi. l. properandum. §. finautem. et 263 ibi not."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, the penalty for crime and adultery is death. <note>original: "xiij. q. v. relegates."</note> But in canon law, an adulterous woman is not killed, but thrust into a monastery. <note>original: "§. qui caueat. C. de adultis. auf. sed hodie."</note> He can also be relegated; it can be spoken of according to the laws that were before the ancient law, which ended, where the adulterer who was incestuous of either sex was punished by the sword. <note>original: "C. de adult. l. quauis. ff. eod. l. si adulterium. cum incestu. in princ."</note>

264 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, he who is punished for crimes is not handed over to ecclesiastical burial. <note>original: "xxiij. q. v. placuit. c. fures."</note> Unless they were contrite in death. <note>original: "xij. q. ij. c. fina."</note> But in civil law, they are not allowed to be buried anywhere unless it was first asked of the prince and granted. <note>original: "ff. de cada. puni. l. j. et ij. et iij."</note>

265 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, no penalty ought to exceed fourfold. <note>original: "insti. de action. §. omnes."</note> But in canon law, justice is found otherwise. <note>original: "xvij. q. iiij. c. quisquis. capitu. cum devotissima. xij. quesstione. ij."</note>

266 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, a minor does not swear, and his oath is null. <note>original: "ff. de iureiurand. l. qui iurasse. et arg. in. l. j. C. de falsa mone. r. l. ij. §. i. C. de iura. calu. et aut. sacramenta puberum. C. si aduer. vendi."</note> It fails in the case where a ward obligates himself from his oath, as if a manumitted person swears to provide services to the manumitter. <note>original: "ff. de lib. causa. l. fina."</note> But in canon law, a ward can swear if he is capable of guile, and if he does not keep the oath, he commits perjury. <note>original: "xxij. q. v. paruuli. et ibi de hoc ego dico, quod satis probabiliter potest defendi, quod etiam iure civili sacramentum pupilli doli capacis valeat, ut not. in. d. c. paruuli."</note>

267 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In canon law, for the very reason that someone enters for the sake of stealing, he is a thief if he is a stranger. <note>original: "in. c. tres psonas. xxiij. q. iiij. et ibi gloss. de penitent. distinctio. ij. si propter. a. c. sequen."</note> But in civil law it is otherwise. <note>original: "ff. de furt. l. vulgari. §. qui furti."</note>

268 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In civil law, he who has promised something that consists in giving under a penalty, if something is omitted to be given, he is held to the whole penalty. <note>original: "ff. si famil. herciscun. l. heredes. §. in illa. l. stipulationes. l. in exectionibus. de verborum obligationi. et plene not. in l. si seruus. §. si plurium. si quis cautio."</note> But in canon law, the exception of Innocent stands in the way; the opinion of Azo follows in the chapter *Sua* regarding penalties, as is fully noted there. <note>original: "c. sua. de penis. ut ibi plene not."</note>

269 ¶ And the Clerk. A difference. In canon law, no one lawfully receives something to point out a thief. <note>original: "c. qui cum fure. extra de fur. j. q. j. ex his vobis, cuibi no."</note> But in civil law

<summary>This page presents a comparative legal analysis of civil law and canon law, highlighting specific differences in judicial procedure, punishment, marital law, and moral obligations.</summary>
<keywords>civil law, canon law, legal differences, ecclesiastical law, excommunication, restitution, matrimony, forgery, criminal punishment, oath, theft</keywords>

Tractatuum volumen primum.

236 ¶ And the Clerk. Concerning civil law, if anyone appeals from a sentence of excommunication while the appeal is pending, he is not excommunicated, for by the appeal the pronouncement is rescinded. <note>original: "l. j. in fine. ff. ad turpilianum"</note> And because by the making of an appeal he is exempted from the jurisdiction of him who passed the sentence, it does not bind him in the meantime. <note>original: "l. si. ff. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum. l. si a non competenti"</note> However, one is permitted to appeal even from a sentence that carries execution with it. <note>original: "ff. de poenis. l. qui ad statuam. l. qui ultimo"</note> In canon law, however, a distinction is made: either the excess was committed in the day, or under a condition; then, if he appeals, the effect of the excommunication does not persist in the meantime. Or it is passed absolutely, and in this case he remains excommunicated even if an appeal is pending. <note>original: "c. praeterea. c. pastoralis. de appellationibus"</note>

237 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, while a request for <term>restitutio in integrum</term> <gloss>restoration to the original state</gloss> is pending, nothing is to be innovated, nor is the sentence to be sent for execution in the meantime. <note>original: "C. nil novari in integrum restitutione pendente. in rubrica magis"</note> But in canon law, the sentence is sent for execution while the question of <term>restitutio in integrum</term> is pending, provided that a security is interposed for the revoking of everything backwards, if it should happen that the benefit of restoration is granted. <note>original: "c. sciscitata. de in integrum restitutione"</note> Or concerning this, there was a presumption against the petitioner to be restored to the original state, as is noted in the said chapter <term>Sciscitata</term> and to this effect see the chapter <term>De falsis</term>, law <term>Satis</term>.

238 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, if several are in discord, the sentence of the majority prevails. <note>original: "ff. de re iudicata. l. duo ex tribus"</note> But in canon law it is not so, for in a criminal case the sentence of the majority does not suffice, even if twelve were of a concordant opinion. <note>original: "v. q. viij. si quis episcopus. no. de reg. iur. in vj."</note>

239 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In canon law, prescription runs during the entire time of the malice of the one alienating or squandering. <note>original: "xv. q. iij. si sacerdotes"</note> But in civil law, we do not have good faith if prescription runs immediately after the alienation. <note>original: "aut quas actiones. C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis"</note> ¶ And the Clerk. Concerning civil law, those things which are held by enemies are granted to the occupiers, and those things which are in the goods of no one. <note>original: "insti. de re. di. §. item lapilli"</note> But in canon law, in places held by Roman enemies, another bishop cannot occupy a diocese or his own parish unless it is granted to him by a superior. <note>original: "c. cum de perba. tibi per Innocentium"</note> ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. Whoever flees in a public war is punished capitally by civil law. <note>original: "ff. de re militari. l. omnem."</note> 242 §. <term>q. in acie</term> <gloss>when in the battle line</gloss>. But in canon law he is infamous. <note>original: "vj. q. j. infames"</note> ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. If anyone has bequeathed in a legacy something that is blocked, he delivers it so that it may be the slave of enemies. <note>original: "ff. de legationibus. l. si"</note> But in canon law he is excommunicated. <note>original: "xxiij. q. ult. si quis"</note> ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, if anyone has changed the cause of his possession for himself, the laws we have take place. <note>original: "C. de acquir. possess. l. cum nemo. s. l. ex liberis. et que in eis notatur"</note> But in canon law, if anyone has changed the cause of possession in basilicas, he is to be deprived of his benefices as an unworthy person. <note>original: "c. illud. de excess. praela"</note>

244 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, a blasphemer is punished with the ultimate penalty, as in the <term>Authenticum</term> concerning those who act against nature. <note>original: "ut in aut. ut non luxu. contra naturam"</note> But in canon law, he is excommunicated, and if he is a cleric, he is deposed. <note>original: "xvij. q. iiij. c. si quis"</note> Through chapters it also imposes a penalty as is handed down concerning cursing clerics. <note>original: "c. si quis in otio"</note>

245 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, if anyone uses false instruments and repents, he is not punished for falsehood. <note>original: "C. de fal. l. falsos"</note> In canon law, it is otherwise regarding apostolic letters. <note>original: "c. cura. c. ad falsariorum. de fal."</note> If the letters are not of simple justice. <note>original: "c. accedens"</note>

246 <term>De falsis</term> <gloss>Concerning forgeries</gloss>. ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, the crime of rape is committed against a betrothed woman. <note>original: "C. de rap. virg. l. j."</note> But in canon law, it is otherwise. <note>original: "extra de raptoribus. c. cum causam"</note>

247 <note>original: "ar. xxvij. q. ij. §. j."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. In civil law, he who has corrupted a virgin is heavily punished, yet he is not compelled to take her as a wife; rather, the force of matrimony between them is prohibited, in the <term>Authenticum</term> concerning the rape of women. <note>original: "in aut. de rap. muli."</note> But in canon law, he is compelled to receive her as a wife 248 <note>original: "re. c. h. de adul."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, a most bitter penalty is imposed upon the killer of children. <note>original: "l. j. C. de his qui par. vel libe. occi."</note> But in the canon, he is not so punished. <note>original: "as in c. de infantibus. de his qui filios occiderunt"</note> ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, the penalty for falsehood is deportation and the confiscation of all goods, and this is for a free man; for a slave, it is the ultimate penalty. <note>original: "l. j. §. ult. ff. de fal fis"</note> But in the canons, the penalty for falsehood is manifold, according to how many falsehoods there are, as <term>Hostiensis</term> notes in his <term>Summa</term> concerning falsehoods. <note>original: "§. poena falsi"</note>

250 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, he who has ceded his goods can recover them in their entirety. <note>original: "ff. qui bonis cede. pnt. l. is qui"</note> But in canon law, having obtained the license to cede episcopal dignity, he is compelled to cede. <note>original: "c. quidam. de renunciatione tibi 251 reddidit rō iter."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, fame alone would not impede a marriage from being followed, because when there is not full proof, but semi-proof. <note>original: "ff. de testa. l. ij. not. in l. in bone fidei. C. de iureiur."</note> But in canon law, public fame alone, which has known the blood relation of the future bride or wife, would impede the matrimony from being contracted. <note>original: "c. super eo. de consangui. et affini. c. cum intua. de sponsalibus"</note>

252 <note>original: "fall."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. The voice of one witness in civil law does not impede matrimony from being contracted. <note>original: "l. iurisiurandi. C. de testibus"</note> But in canon law, if the mother alone of the other person wishing to contract matrimony asserts blood relation between them, it impedes the matrimony. <note>original: "c. sup eo. de testibus"</note> ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, there is a certain penalty of the mines, where those who are condemned to the mine are bound with heavier shackles. Others are in the work of the mine, and these are bound with lighter ones; both of these lose their citizenship and liberty. Others, however, are condemned to the service of the miners and serve entirely in the mines, and these lose their citizenship but not their liberty; and this is done when they are condemned for a time. If, however, it is in perpetuity, they lose both, namely citizenship and liberty. <note>original: "ff. de pe. l. aut damna. §. cui poena"</note> In canon law, such penalties are not found imposed, nor should they be imposed. <note>original: "c. de calumniatis"</note> But the penalty of prison can be equated to these penalties, which the Church inflicts for grave crimes. <note>original: "c. plene. r. c. ff. de hereticis"</note> And the penalty by which one is reduced to servitude, or is handed over to the court to serve. <note>original: "xvij. q. iiij. c. si quis. xj. q. j. statuimus"</note> Otherwise he is sold. <note>original: "l. r. vi. de clerici."</note>

254 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, a boy or girl of seven years who attempted to have carnal knowledge, and perhaps could not due to the imbecility of age, through this induces the justice of public decency, so that matrimony cannot be contracted. <note>original: "c. iuvenis. de sponsalibus"</note> But in civil law it is not found among the causes that impede matrimony; which causes are enumerated in law 3, Digest concerning nuptials, near the end, and in the Institutes concerning nuptials. <note>original: "D. de nupt. circa finem. et insti. de nupt. §. h."</note> And similarly, if a brother betrothed someone in fact, who by law could not, due to blood relation impeding it with the other brother, he cannot contract matrimony. <note>original: "c. ad audientiam. de sponsalibus"</note> But in civil law, it is not the case that there is any bond impeding blood relation through prior betrothals, for concerning an impossible thing there is no obligation. <note>original: "§. si impossibile. insti. de inuti. stipula."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, delay does not regularly occur by the thing itself, but by an interpellation made in a suitable place and time. <note>original: "ff. de usur. l. mora. in princ."</note> And there it fails in the cases noted there. But in canon law, delay occurs by the thing itself in the slow payment of tithes. <note>original: "xvj. q. j. in 256 decime. not. in. c. cum homines. de decimis."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, simple fornication is not punished, but rather permitted. <note>original: "l. in concubunatu. ff. de concubi. l. ij. C. de donat. inter virum et uxorem"</note> By canon law, any fornication is prohibited. <note>original: "xxiij. q. iiij. nemo sibi. et ibi not."</note>

257 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, matrimony is dissolved if one of the spouses wishes to enter a monastery, and does enter. <note>original: "in aut. de nup. §. dissolvatur"</note> 258 But in the canon, it is otherwise. <note>original: "xxvij. q. ij. Agatosa"</note> ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, nuptials can be contracted between first cousins. <note>original: "C. de nup. l. in celebrandis. q. non. l. iij. ca. q. ij. qui attinet sibi in quarto gradu consanguinitatis vel affinitatis, prohibetur contrahere matrimonium. c. non est de consangui. et affini."</note>

259 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, paternal power lasts throughout the entire age of the son. But in canon law, paternal power is dissolved upon reaching adult age regarding carnal and spiritual matrimony, which pertains to an oath. <note>original: "xx. q. ij. puella. xxiij. q. iij. tribus not. xxij. q. v. honoretur"</note>

260 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, it is not permitted for a man to beat his wife. <note>original: "l. cosenſu. C. de repudijs"</note> Nevertheless, he can correct her. <note>original: "vij. q. j. scilicet alterius. l. respiciendum. ff. de penis"</note> But in the canon, it is permitted to clerics only to guard their sinning wives, to bind them, and to compel them to fast, yet not to mortify them. <note>original: "xxiij. q. iiij. placuit"</note> And there is a reason regarding clerics that is stronger than in others, as is noted there.

261 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, a wife cannot vow continence, nor can the opposite, without the license of the other spouse. <note>original: "xxxiij. q. v. c. j. et ij."</note> By canon law, it is otherwise: because the matrimony is broken if one wishes to vow chastity. <note>original: "in aut. de nup. §. dissolvatur"</note>

262 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In canon law, if anyone proposes a peremptory exception after the intention of the actor has been established, and it happens that he fails in the proof of that exception, he is condemned to the actor in expenses. <note>original: "c. finem litibus. et ibi not. de dolo et contuma"</note> But in civil law, this which is said concerning the condemnation of expenses does not have a place, except in cases, so that the loser is condemned to the winner in expenses. <note>original: "C. de iudi. l. properandum. §. finautem. et 263 ibi not."</note> ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, the penalty for wickedness and adultery is death. <note>original: "xiij. q. v. relegates"</note> But in canon law, the adulterous woman is not killed, but thrust into a monastery. <note>original: "§. qui caueat. C. de adultis. auf. sed hodie"</note> He can also be relegated, he can speak according to the laws that were before the ancient law, the ends of which swore that the adulterer and the incestuous of either sex were punished by the sword. <note>original: "C. de adult. l. quauis. ff. eod. l. si adulterium. cum incestu. in princ."</note>

264 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, he who has been killed for his crimes is not handed over for ecclesiastical burial. <note>original: "xxiij. q. v. placuit. c. fures"</note> Unless they were contrite in death. <note>original: "xij. q. ij. c. fina."</note> But in civil law, they are not allowed to be buried anywhere unless it was first requested from the prince and granted. <note>original: "ff. de cada. puni. l. j. et ij. et iij."</note>

265 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, no penalty ought to exceed the quadruple. <note>original: "insti. de action. §. omnes"</note> But in canon law, justice is found otherwise according to his judgment. <note>original: "xvij. q. iiij. c. quisquis. capitu. cum devotissima. xij. quesstione. ij."</note>

266 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, a person under puberty does not swear, and his oath is null. <note>original: "ff. de iureiurand. l. qui iurasse. et arg. in. l. j. C. de falsa mone. r. l. ij. §. i. C. de iura. calu. et aut. sacramenta puberum. C. si aduer. vendi."</note> It fails in the case where the ward obligates himself by his oath, as if one who is manumitted swears to perform services for the manumitter. <note>original: "ff. de lib. causa. l. fina."</note> But in canon law, a ward can swear if he is capable of guile, and if he does not keep the oath, he is perjured. <note>original: "xxij. q. v. paruuli. et ibi de hoc ego dico, quod satis probabiliter potest defendi, quod etiam iure civili sacramentum pupilli doli capacis valeat, ut not. in. d. c. paruuli."</note>

267 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In canon law, by the very fact that someone enters for the purpose of stealing, he is a thief, if he is a stranger. <note>original: "in. c. tres psonas. xxiij. q. iiij. et ibi gloss. de penitent. distinctio. ij. si propter. a. c. sequen."</note> But in civil law it is otherwise, as is the text in the Digest concerning theft. <note>original: "ff. de furt. l. vulgari. §. qui furti"</note>

268 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In civil law, he who has promised something that consists in giving under a penalty, if anything is omitted to be given, he is held to the whole penalty. <note>original: "ff. si famil. herciscun. l. heredes. §. in illa. l. stipulationes. l. in exectionibus. de verborum obligationi. et plene not. in l. si seruus. §. si plurium. si quis cautio."</note> But in canon law the exception of <term>Innocent</term> opposes this. The opinion of <term>Azo</term> follows in the chapter <term>Sua</term> concerning penalties, as is fully noted there. <note>original: "c. sua. de penis"</note>

269 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. In canon law, no one licitly receives anything to indicate a thief. <note>original: "c. qui cum fure. extra de fur. j. q. j. ex his vobis, cuibi no."</note> But in civil law...
