Tractatuum volumen primum.

236 ¶ And the Clerk. Regarding civil law, if someone appeals a sentence of excommunication while the appeal is pending, they are not excommunicated, for the pronouncement is rescinded by the appeal. Law 1, at the end, Digest, *ad turpilianum* <note>Referring to the Senatus Consultum Turpilianum regarding false accusations.</note>. And because the appeal has been made, one is exempted from the jurisdiction of the one who passed sentence, and it does not bind them in the meantime. Law "if," Digest, *de iurisdictione omnium iudicum* <gloss>concerning the jurisdiction of all judges</gloss>. Law "if from one not competent." However, one may also appeal from a sentence that carries execution with it. Digest, *de poenis* <gloss>concerning penalties</gloss>. Law "who to the statue," Law "who finally." By canon law, however, a distinction is made: either the excess was in the day <note>Refers to a procedural error or a time-bound condition.</note>, or under a condition; then, if they appeal, the effect of the excommunication does not persist in the interim. Or it is issued purely, and in this case, the excommunicated party remains so even if an appeal is pending. Chapter *praeterea*, Chapter *pastoralis*, *de appellationibus* <gloss>concerning appeals</gloss>.

237 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, nothing is to be innovated while a request for *restitutio in integrum* <gloss>restoration to original state</gloss> is pending, nor is the sentence to be sent for execution in the meantime. Code, *nil novari in integrum restitutione pendente* <gloss>nothing new while restoration is pending</gloss>, in the rubric, rather. By canon law, the sentence is ordered for execution while a question of *restitutio in integrum* is pending, provided that security is posted to revoke everything retroactively if the benefit of restoration happens to be granted. Chapter *sciscitata*, *de in integrum restitutione*. Or regarding the fact that there was a presumption there against the one seeking to be restored to their original state, as noted in the said chapter *sciscitata*. And to this point, Code, *de falsis* <gloss>concerning forgeries</gloss>, Law "enough."

238 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, if several are in disagreement, the sentence of the majority prevails. Digest, *de re iudicata* <gloss>concerning adjudicated matters</gloss>, Law "two out of three." But by canon law, it is not so, for in a criminal case, the sentence of the majority does not suffice, even if twelve were in accord. Question 5, 8, Chapter *si quis episcopus* <gloss>if any bishop</gloss>. Note, *de reg. iur.* <gloss>concerning rules of law</gloss>, in the sixth [book of Decretals].

239 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By canon law, prescription runs throughout the time of the wrongdoing of the one alienating or squandering. Question 15, 3, Chapter *si sacerdotes* <gloss>if priests</gloss>. But by civil law, we do not have good faith if prescription runs immediately after alienation. Or "which actions," Code, *de sacrosanctis ecclesiis* <gloss>concerning holy churches</gloss>. ¶ And the Clerk. By civil law, those things held by enemies are granted to the occupants, as are those things in the property of no one. Institutes, *de re. di.* <gloss>concerning the division of things</gloss>, section "item pebbles." But by canon law, in places held by Roman enemies, another bishop cannot occupy a diocese or his parish unless it is granted to him by a superior. Chapter *cum de perba.* <gloss>concerning the verb</gloss>, by Innocent. ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. Whoever flees in public war is punished by capital punishment by civil law. Digest, *de re militari* <gloss>concerning military matters</gloss>, Law "every."

242 Section "if in the battle line." But by canon law, they are infamous. Question 6, 1, *infames*. ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. If someone bequeaths in a legacy <unclear>impeditat</unclear>, they trade so that it may be the slave of enemies. Digest, *de legationibus* <gloss>concerning embassies</gloss>, Law "if." But by canon law, they are excommunicated. Question 23, last, *si quis* <gloss>if someone</gloss>. ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, if someone has changed the cause of their possession for themselves, the laws we have apply. Code, *de acquir. possess.* <gloss>concerning acquiring possession</gloss>, Law "when no one," section Law "from children," and what is noted in them. But by canon law, if someone has changed the cause of their possession in cathedrals, they must be deprived of their benefits as unworthy. Chapter *illud*, *de excess. praela.* <gloss>concerning the excess of prelates</gloss>.

244 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, a blasphemer is punished by the ultimate penalty, as in the Authentic, "that there be no luxury against nature." But by canon law, they are excommunicated, and if a cleric, they are deposed. Question 17, 4, Chapter *si quis* <gloss>if someone</gloss>, through chapters [it] also imposes punishment as handed down concerning cursing clerics, Chapter *si quis in otio* <gloss>if someone is at leisure</gloss>.

245 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, if someone uses false instruments and repents, they are not punished for forgery. Code, *de fal.* <gloss>concerning forgery</gloss>, Law "false." In canon law, it is otherwise regarding apostolic letters. Chapter *cura*, Chapter *ad falsariorum*, *de fal.* <gloss>concerning forgery</gloss>, if only the letters are not of simple justice. Chapter *accedens*.

246 *de falsis*. ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, the crime of rape is committed against a betrothed woman. Code, *de rap. virg.* <gloss>concerning rape of a virgin</gloss>, Law 1. But by canon law, it is otherwise, *extra de raptoribus* <gloss>outside: concerning abductors</gloss>, Chapter *cum causam*.

247 [Reference to] Question 27, 2, section 1. ¶ And the Clerk. By civil law, whoever has corrupted a virgin is severely punished, yet he is not compelled to take her as a wife; rather, it is prohibited by the force of matrimony between them, in the Authentic, *de rap. muli.* <gloss>concerning rape of women</gloss>. But by canon law, he is driven to receive her as a wife. 248 [reference to] Chapter *h.* <gloss>this</gloss>, *de adul.* <gloss>concerning adultery</gloss>. ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, the most severe penalty is imposed on the murderer of children. Law 1, Code, *de his qui par. vel libe. occi.* <gloss>concerning those who kill parents or children</gloss>. But in the canon, it does not punish in that way, as in the Chapter *de infantibus* <gloss>concerning infants</gloss>, *de his qui filios occiderunt* <gloss>concerning those who killed their children</gloss>. ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, the penalty for forgery is deportation and the confiscation of all goods, and this for a free person; for a slave, however, it is the ultimate punishment. Law 1, section last, Digest, *de fal fis.* <gloss>concerning forgery</gloss>. But truly, the canons have a multiple penalty for forgery, according to how many types of forgery there are, as Hostien notes in his *Summa*, *de falsis*, section "penalty of forgery."

250 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, whoever has ceded goods can recover them in their entirety. Digest, *qui bonis cede. pnt.* <gloss>concerning those who cede goods</gloss>, Law "he who." But by canon law, having obtained permission to cede the episcopal dignity, he is compelled to cede. Chapter *quidam*, *de renunciatione* <gloss>concerning resignation</gloss>, [where it] rendered the path for you. 251 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, fame alone would not impede matrimony to be obeyed, because when there is not full proof, but half-proof. Digest, *de testa.* <gloss>concerning testaments</gloss>, Law 2, noted in Law "in good faith," Code, *de iureiur.* <gloss>concerning oaths</gloss>. But by canon law, public fame alone, which knew the consanguinity of the future spouse of the wife, would impede a marriage from being contracted. Chapter *super eo*, *de consangui. et affini.* <gloss>concerning consanguinity and affinity</gloss>, Chapter *cum intua*, *de sponsalibus* <gloss>concerning betrothals</gloss>.

252 [Reference to] error. ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. The word of one witness by civil law does not impede matrimony from being contracted. Law "oath," Code, *de testibus* <gloss>concerning witnesses</gloss>. But by canon law, if the mother alone of another wishing to contract matrimony asserts consanguinity between them, it impedes the matrimony. Chapter *sup eo*, *de testibus*. ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, there is a certain penalty of the mines, and those who condemn to the mine are afflicted with heavier chains. Others are in the work of the mine, and these are afflicted with lighter ones; both of these lose citizenship and liberty. Others, however, are condemned to the service of the miners, and they serve entirely in the mines, and these lose citizenship but not liberty; and this is done for the time they are condemned. If truly for perpetuity, they lose both, that is, citizenship and liberty. Digest, *de pe.* <gloss>concerning penalties</gloss>, Law "or condemn," section "to whom penalty." If by canon law such penalties are not found imposed, nor should they be imposed. Chapter *de calumniatis* <gloss>concerning those falsely accused</gloss>. But to these penalties can be equated the penalty of prison, which the church inflicts for grave crimes, Chapter *plene*, etc. Chapter, Digest, *de hereticis* <gloss>concerning heretics</gloss>. And the penalty by which one is reduced to slavery. Question 17, 4, Chapter *si quis* <gloss>if someone</gloss>. Or is handed over to the court to serve. Question 11, 1, *statuimus* <gloss>we establish</gloss>. Otherwise, they are sold. Law 1, 6, *de clerici* <gloss>concerning clerics</gloss>.

254 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, a youth or girl <column-break/> who has attempted to know, and perhaps could not because of the weakness of age, by this introduces the justice of public honesty, so that matrimony cannot be contracted. Chapter *iuvenis*, *de sponsalibus*. But by civil law, it is not found among the causes that impede matrimony, which causes are enumerated in Law 3, Digest, *de nupt.* <gloss>concerning nuptials</gloss>, around the end, and Institutes, *de nupt.*, section "h." And similarly, if a brother has betrothed someone de facto, who by law could not, due to impeding consanguinity with the other brother, he cannot contract matrimony. Chapter *ad audientiam*, *de sponsalibus*. But by civil law, it is not that there is any bond impeding consanguinity through prior betrothal, for to the impossible there is no obligation. Section "if impossible," Institutes, *de inuti. stipula.* <gloss>concerning useless stipulations</gloss>. ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, regularly, delay is not made by the thing itself, but by an interpellation made in a suitable place and time. Digest, *de usur.* <gloss>concerning usury</gloss>, Law "delay," in the beginning, and it fails there in the cases noted there. But by canon law, delay is made by the thing itself in the late payment of tithes. Question 16, 1, *in decime*. Noted in Chapter *cum homines*, *de decimis* <gloss>concerning tithes</gloss>. ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, simple fornication is not punished, rather it is permitted. Law "in concubinage," Digest, *de concubi.* <gloss>concerning concubines</gloss>, Law 2, Code, *de donat. inter virum et uxorem* <gloss>concerning donations between husband and wife</gloss>. By canon law, any fornication is prohibited. Question 23, 4, *nemo sibi* <gloss>no one to himself</gloss>, and noted there.

257 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, matrimony is dissolved if one of the spouses wishes to enter a monastery, and does enter. In the Authentic, *de nup.*, section "is dissolved." 258 But in the canon, it is otherwise. Question 27, 2, *Agatosa*. ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, nuptials can be contracted between cousins. Code, *de nup.*, Law "in celebrating." Question 3, 2, who relates to themselves in the fourth degree of consanguinity or affinity, it is prohibited to contract matrimony. Chapter *non est*, *de consangui. et affini.*

259 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, paternal power lasts throughout the entire age of the son. But by canon law, paternal power is dissolved upon reaching adult age regarding carnal and spiritual matrimony, which is regarding the oath. Question 20, 2, *puella*. Question 23, 3, *tribus* noted. Question 22, 5, *honoretur* <gloss>let him be honored</gloss>.

260 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, a man is not permitted to beat his wife. Law "consent," Code, *de repudijs* <gloss>concerning repudiations</gloss>. Yet he can correct her, as in Question 7, 1, *scilicet alterius* <gloss>namely of another</gloss>. Law "to be looked at," Digest, *de penis*. But in the canon, it is permitted only to clerics to guard their wives who sin, to bind them, and to compel them to fast, yet not to mortify them. Question 23, 4, *placuit* <gloss>it pleased</gloss>. And the reason is stronger in clerics than in others, as noted there.

261 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, a wife cannot vow continence, nor the opposite, without the license of the other spouse. Question 33, 5, Chapter 1 and 2. By canon law, it is otherwise, because matrimony is broken if one wishes to vow chastity in the Authentic, *de nup.*, section "is dissolved."

262 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By canon law, if someone proposes a peremptory exception after the plaintiff's intention has been established, and it happens that they fail in the proof of that exception, they are condemned to the plaintiff in expenses. Chapter *finem litibus* <gloss>end to lawsuits</gloss>, and noted there, *de dolo et contuma.* <gloss>concerning fraud and contumacy</gloss>. But by civil law, this which is said concerning the condemnation of expenses does not have a place, except in cases, so that the vanquished is condemned to the victor in expenses. Code, *de iudi.* <gloss>concerning judgments</gloss>, Law "to be hurried," section "if finally," and 263 noted there. ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, the penalty for crime and adultery is death. Question 13, 5, *relegates*. But by canon law, an adulterous woman is not killed, but thrust into a monastery. Section "who takes care," Code, *de adultis*. Authentic, "but today." She can also be relegated, [and] can speak according to the laws that were before the ancient law, the ends which are sworn adulterous, [and] which incestuous of either sex were punished by the sword. Code, *de adult.*, Law "whichever," Digest, of the same, Law "if adultery," with incest, in the beginning.

264 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, one who is punished by death for crimes is not handed over for ecclesiastical burial. Question 23, 5, *placuit*, Chapter *fures* <gloss>thieves</gloss>, unless they were contrite in death. Question 12, 2, Chapter *fina.* But by civil law, they are not allowed to be buried anywhere unless it has first been asked of the prince and granted. Digest, *de cada. puni.* <gloss>concerning corpses of the punished</gloss>, Law 1, 2, and 3.

265 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, no penalty ought to exceed quadruple. Institutes, *de action.*, section "all." But by canon law, justice is found otherwise, *sue dente*. Question 17, 4, Chapter *quisquis* <gloss>whoever</gloss>, Chapter *cum devotissima* <gloss>with most devout</gloss>, Question 12, 2.

266 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, an impubescent does not swear, and their oath is null. Digest, *de iureiurand.*, Law "who has sworn." And argument in Law 1, Code, *de falsa mone.* <gloss>concerning false money</gloss>, Law 2, section 1, Code, *de iura. calu.* <gloss>concerning the oath of calumny</gloss>, and the Authentic, "sacraments of the pubescents," Code, *si aduer. vendi.* <gloss>if against sales</gloss>. It fails in the case where the ward binds themselves by their oath, as if one manumitted swears to perform works for the manumittor. Digest, *de lib. causa.* <gloss>concerning free cause</gloss>, Law *fina.* But by canon law, a ward can swear if they are capable of guile, and if they do not keep the oath, they perjure themselves. Question 22, 5, *paruuli* <gloss>little ones</gloss>, and there concerning this I say that it can be defended quite probably that the sacrament of a ward capable of guile is also valid by civil law, as noted in the said Chapter *paruuli*.

267 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By canon law, by the very fact that someone enters for the sake of stealing, they are a thief if they are a foreigner. In Chapter *tres psonas* <gloss>three persons</gloss>, Question 23, 4, and the gloss there, *de penitent.*, distinction 2, *si propter*, and the following chapter. But by civil law, it is otherwise, as is the text in Digest, *de furt.* <gloss>concerning theft</gloss>, Law "vulgar," section "who of theft."

268 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By civil law, whoever has promised something that consists in giving under a penalty, if something is omitted to be given, they are held to the whole penalty. Digest, *si famil. herciscun.* <gloss>if the family is to be divided</gloss>, Law "heirs," section "in that," Law "stipulations," Law "in executions," *de verborum obligationi.* <gloss>concerning verbal obligations</gloss>, and fully noted in Law "if slave," section "if of many," if anyone security. But by canon law, the exception of Innocent stands in the way. The opinion of Azo follows in Chapter *sua*, *de penis*, as fully noted there.

269 ¶ And the Clerk. Difference. By canon law, no one lawfully receives anything to indicate a thief. Chapter *qui cum fure* <gloss>who with a thief</gloss>, *extra de fur.* <gloss>outside: concerning theft</gloss>, 1, 1, *ex his vobis* <gloss>from these to you</gloss>, where [it is] noted.
